planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil with some direct sun to keep the gold coloring vivid.

directions: Latifolia Maculata is a large, old English boxwood form grown for its broad, leathery leaves that emerge bright golden yellow in spring before settling into dark green blotched with dull yellow through summer. It builds slowly into a substantial rounded shrub or small standard, taking many years to reach full size, and can be left loosely pruned or clipped into large-scale topiary. Some direct sun is needed to keep the variegation bright, since deep shade causes the gold markings to fade toward plain green. It has held a long-standing reputation in English gardens as one of the showiest variegated boxwood forms.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil sheltered from harsh winter sun and wind; stake young plants to establish an upright leader.

directions: Aurea Pendula is a distinctive, slow-growing English boxwood form with upright branches that arch and droop irregularly at their tips, giving mature specimens an unusual sculptural silhouette rather than the dense mounded shape typical of most boxwood. The stems and leaves are heavily streaked and splashed with bright gold variegation against green, most vivid on new growth. Left largely unpruned it develops the most character, though light shaping can control size; afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch in hot climates. It is best used as a specimen or accent plant where its weeping form and gold coloring can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; tolerates heat and drought better than most English boxwood selections.

directions: Hiram Saunders arose as a branch sport of common boxwood and stands out for its notably compact, low growth habit and smaller, glossy dark leaves compared to typical Buxus sempervirens. Where standard English boxwood forms can reach several feet within a decade, this cultivar stays noticeably lower and denser, needing less frequent shearing to hold a tidy shape. It has proven better suited than many boxwood selections to hot, humid Southern growing conditions, tolerating heat and drought once established while retaining good pest and disease resistance. It works well as a low hedge or foundation planting in warmer zones where English boxwood otherwise struggles.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; its rapid growth makes it useful for establishing tall screens quickly.

directions: Highlander is a naturally occurring sport of common boxwood selected for its rapid, upright, pyramidal growth, reportedly the fastest-growing of the English boxwood types, often gaining close to two feet of height per year once established. The small leaves stay a deep, glossy dark green through all seasons with little of the bronze winter discoloration common in older boxwood forms. Its speed and tall, narrow habit make it well suited to building a formal screen or tall hedge faster than traditional English boxwood cultivars, and it shows good general tolerance of heat, sun, and common boxwood pests. Shear it two or three times a season while young to encourage denser branching if a tighter hedge form is wanted.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to shade; selected for reliable performance in colder climates where many boxwood cultivars fail.

directions: Arctic Emerald was discovered as a cold-tolerant mutation of common boxwood and is valued for combining unusually reliable winter hardiness with a faster growth rate than most cold-hardy boxwood selections. The glossy, deep green foliage carries a faint bluish cast and holds its color through winter without the bronzing or burn that affects many boxwood in exposed, cold sites. Its columnar to pyramidal habit adapts to sun, partial sun, or shade, making it a flexible choice for hedging or specimen use well into colder hardiness zones than traditional English or American boxwood. Light annual shearing keeps the naturally upright form dense and tidy.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; among the most winter-hardy boxwood available, suited to sites too cold for most cultivars.

directions: Polar was selected from a boxwood that survived decades of severe Scandinavian winters and is grown specifically for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating far lower temperatures than typical English or Korean boxwood cultivars. The dense, medium-textured habit carries shiny, dark green, broadly elliptic leaves that show little to no winter bronzing even after hard freezes. It also displays notably good resistance to common boxwood diseases compared with older cultivars, making it a dependable choice for formal hedging or topiary in regions where winter injury has ruled out other boxwood. Its compact growth needs only light shearing to maintain a clean form.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade; a good disease-resistant alternative where boxwood blight or winter injury limits other cultivars.

directions: Green Ice is a hybrid boxwood combining English and Korean boxwood parentage, grown for its dense, upright columnar habit and small, glossy, deep green leaves that emerge with a blue-green cast in spring. It holds its rich winter color well and needs comparatively little pruning to keep a neat, mounded form, making it useful for low hedges, borders, and foundation plantings. Breeders have noted markedly better resistance to boxwood blight in this hybrid than in traditional English boxwood, making it a sound substitute where blight pressure is a concern. It performs reliably in both full sun and light shade once established.
